diagrams.title: Moving Off Fully Insured Without Getting Burned
diagrams.subtitle: Five practitioner steps from renewal math to a self-funded future
diagrams.caption: Practitioners sequence the funding switch around loss-ratio math, written surplus terms, complete IMQ paperwork, a modeled year-two downside, and a claims-experience harvest that opens traditional self-funding.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Step order is an editorial sequence of separate practitioner tips and gates. Every figure is an attributed practitioner claim and varies by contract and carrier.
diagrams.note: Sources are Dr. Eric Bricker (AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained), Tyler Dutchover, Warp, and Maximize Asset Protection.

stages.label: Run Loss-Ratio Math on Renewal
stages.detail: A 120-employee Dallas group at a 60% loss ratio got a flat renewal and no refund, leaving roughly $560,000 of about $1.4 million in premium with the carrier (Dr. Eric Bricker).

stages.label: Lock Surplus Split in Writing
stages.detail: Level-funded contracts return 50% to 80% of the leftover claims fund as cash or lower rates, depending on the specific contract (Tyler Dutchover).

stages.label: Collect Every IMQ
stages.detail: Some carriers require an Individual Medical Questionnaire taking three to five minutes per employee. Warp says typical brokers skip level funding over the extra work, while Warp has produced quotes showing 60% plus savings.

stages.label: Model the Year-Two Laser
stages.detail: Price a renewal laser that pushes one employee's specific attachment to $200,000, plus the 10 percent or higher fully insured fallback rate (Tyler Dutchover).

stages.label: Harvest Claims Experience for Self-Funding
stages.detail: Allstate will look at traditional self-funding for groups under 100 lives that arrive with level-funded claims proof, provided the business can write a check for the full aggregate within a couple of months (Maximize Asset Protection).

diagrams.title: Where an Amlodipine Dollar Goes
diagrams.subtitle: Generic Norvasc priced off AWP versus what the drug actually costs
diagrams.caption: An AWP-discount contract bills the plan 48 cents for a generic the pharmacy acquires for 1.9 cents, so the plan pays almost exactly 25 times acquisition cost.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Single-drug walk-through as presented by the practitioner. The PBM and pharmacy margins are each stated as about 23 cents and are rounded.
diagrams.note: Source is Dr. Eric Bricker, AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained (0XFk1m3yGuY at 00.03.09).

stages.label: Average Wholesale Price Benchmark
stages.detail: AWP for amlodipine used as the pricing base in the PBM contract.

stages.label: Billed to Plan at 20% of AWP
stages.detail: The percentage-off-AWP discount looks steep yet hides the real gap.

stages.label: PBM Retained Spread
stages.conversion: About half of the billed amount
stages.detail: The PBM profits about 23 cents on the fill.

stages.label: Pharmacy Retained Margin
stages.conversion: About half of the billed amount
stages.detail: The pharmacy also profits about 23 cents on the fill.

stages.label: Pharmacy Acquisition Cost
stages.detail: The pharmacy acquires the drug for 1.9 cents.

diagrams.title: What a Laser Really Costs
diagrams.subtitle: Named-claimant exposure above the specific deductible, and the ag-spec counter
diagrams.caption: A $600,000 laser over a $150,000 specific deductible quietly adds up to $450,000 of exposure, while a near-spec laser can be traded away with an aggregating specific.
diagrams.assumptions_note: The $25,000 gap is arithmetic on the $125,000 laser and $100,000 specific deductible cited by Spencer Smith. Carriers often accept the $50,000 ag spec trade only when the laser sits that close to the spec.
diagrams.note: Sources are Benefit Whisperer (6E1eObzSNLc at 00.01.05) and Spencer Smith of Self-Funded (VatFfWseBbI at 00.07.48).

diagrams.title: Level-Funding Economics in Practitioner Numbers
diagrams.subtitle: Refunds, attachment, savings, and market share reported by operators
diagrams.caption: Level-funding operators report refunds of unused claim dollars, a 125% aggregate attachment, premium savings of 45% to 60% plus, and mid-market share climbing to 45% of lives.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Where a single figure was reported, min, max, and typical are set equal. The SHP typical refund is the stated current 66% inside the stated 60% to 100% market range.
diagrams.note: Sources are Security Health Plan, BeneSmart (Rich), Warp, and Dr. Eric Bricker of AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained.

bars.label: SHP Refund on Unused Claim Dollars
bars.display: 66% now, inside a 60% to 100% market range

bars.label: Level-Funded Share in 50-500 Groups
bars.display: About 10% ten years ago to 45% today

diagrams.title: Four Gates Before Signing a PBM Contract
diagrams.subtitle: Following the money from plan-billed price to retained rebate
diagrams.caption: Each gate targets a gap the buyer never sees, from AWP-only invoices to narrowed rebate definitions and trade-secret pricing clauses.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Gate order is editorial. Carving out the PBM is available to self-funded sponsors only, since fully insured plans are locked to the carrier's PBM.
diagrams.note: Sources are RxPreferred, Dr. Eric Bricker of AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained, Desai of the American Health Law Association, and Tyler Dutchover.

nodes.question: Does every claim show the pharmacy-paid amount next to the plan-billed amount?
nodes.fail_action: Reject AWP-only invoicing. RxPreferred's case paid the pharmacy $10, invoiced $100 plus a $2 admin fee, and kept $92.

nodes.question: Will the PBM disclose any customer besides the health plan, plus market share and bonus payments?
nodes.fail_action: Demand formulary, market share, and bonus payment disclosure, not just rebates.

nodes.question: Does the rebate definition include all discounts and amounts based on a percentage of drug cost?
nodes.fail_action: Rewrite the definition, since a narrowed rebate creates revenue pockets outside pass-through.

nodes.question: Is the contract free of any clause calling real drug costs confidential trade secrets?
nodes.pass_next: Sign and carve the PBM out of the carrier bundle if self-funded
nodes.fail_action: Strike the clause, and assume overpayment if the PBM refuses to show receipts.

diagrams.title: The Workers' Comp Mod-Control Team
diagrams.subtitle: Who owns claims, reserves, class codes, and return-to-work
diagrams.caption: Practitioners say the most common mistake is that no one monitors claims experience, and some experts believe 60 to 70 percent of mods are wrong.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Role names are structural groupings of practitioner tips. The 60 to 70 percent figure is a belief Gordon Coyle attributes to some experts, not a measured rate.
diagrams.note: Sources are Gordon Coyle of The Coyle Group, Ryan Hanigan of JJ Doorhy & Associates, ClinardInsGroup, and WorkCompConsultants.

center.focus: Gets the last five years of loss runs explained line by line and verifies every open reserve before loss figures go to NCCI, since reserves count the same as paid dollars.

spokes.kpi: Runs tools estimating the mod without one shock loss when a mod above 1.0 threatens bid eligibility with a general contractor.

spokes.type: Carrier with in-house nurses and caseworkers
spokes.kpi: Pushes injured workers back sooner, shifting more of each loss to the frequency side.
Completes class code review and checks subcontractor certificates for excluded owners and clerical-only coverage before the auditor does.
Places workers in doctor-approved light duty, including nonprofit partner placements that keep indemnity dollars off loss runs and out of the mod.

diagrams.title: Where the Captive Health Dollar Sits
diagrams.subtitle: Spend shares, loss-fund cession, and member loss ratio
diagrams.total_range: Percent shares on the bases noted for each bucket
diagrams.caption: Shopping stop-loss each year attacks only about a fifth of total health spend, while captive members cede most of premium to a shared loss fund and see dollars returned.
diagrams.assumptions_note: Buckets use different bases. The first two are shares of total employer health spend, the third is a share of captive premium, and the fourth is the captive loss ratio.
diagrams.note: Sources are Joe Perelli of Captive Resources and CRI results reported on the Christopher Martens panel.

buckets.label: Below-Deductible Claims
buckets.notes: Share of total health spend the employer retains under the specific deductible.

buckets.label: Stop-Loss Premium
buckets.notes: Share of total health spend, the only slice an annual stop-loss shop touches.

buckets.label: Premium Ceded to Member Loss Fund
buckets.notes: Share of captive premium ceded to the member loss fund in CRI programs.

buckets.label: Captive Loss Ratio
buckets.notes: CRI results alongside $35M returned to members over 10 years.

diagrams.title: Workers' Comp Cost and Recovery Roadmap
diagrams.subtitle: Classification, mod levers, first-aid controls, and lien defense
diagrams.caption: Practitioners find the money in classification, mod management, audit documentation, and disciplined lien and clawback defense.
diagrams.assumptions_note: The four-week cadence is an editorial ordering of practitioner gates. No speaker prescribed a weekly schedule, and results depend on state rules and the account.
diagrams.note: Sources are Insurance for Entrepreneurs, Nia Brooks, Joe Stevens of Bridge Safety Consultants via Employers Group, Jeremy Burris, Insurance Brokers of Arizona, Theresa Kenyon of Synergy, and Medical Lien Management.

weeks.title: Classification Check
weeks.deliverable: Class codes matched to real operations. One mental-health program moved from a home health code to a doctor's office code cut premium about 80% on $2.5M payroll.
weeks.gate: Actual time records for any split payroll, or the whole payroll goes to the highest-rated code.

weeks.title: Mod and Credit Levers
weeks.deliverable: Mod impact sized, since a $200k base premium swings from $150k at a 0.75 mod to $300k at 1.50. Credits checked include a 2% safety credit, 5% drug-free workplace credit, and 5% deviated rate.
weeks.gate: Full cooperation with the annual audit, since refusal can cost up to 3x annual premium.

weeks.title: First-Aid and Exit Controls
weeks.deliverable: Clinic dispenses 600 mg ibuprofen instead of 800 mg to keep a first aid from becoming a recordable, and departing employees sign an injury-free statement.
weeks.gate: Claims filed after termination are contested.

weeks.title: Lien and Clawback Defense
weeks.deliverable: 1024(b)(4) request sent to the plan administrator with the $110-per-day penalty as leverage, and lien itemizations audited. Synergy reports 30-78% average reductions.
weeks.gate: No bulk overpayment refund until the timeline, auditor authority, and 12- or 24-month look-back are verified.
